longo.nar: You have a card that pays you back. It also charges you to hold it. And almost nobody has ever put those two numbers side by side.
longo.cap: A card that pays and charges

longo.kicker: This is not about the card
longo.nar: This is not a video about which card is better. It is about what YOUR card did for you last year, which is a different question and a far more useful one.

longo.preco: the fee posts on a date
longo.nar: It also has a deadline. The fee posts on a specific date, and you decide before that date, every year, whether to keep paying it.
The good news is that both numbers already exist, and both are yours. One is what came back to you. The other is what you paid to hold the card.
One of them is easy to find. The other is scattered across twelve months, which is the only reason this is not obvious already.
Nobody runs this for you. The issuer has no reason to, and you have never had the two numbers in front of you at the same time.
This is not a budgeting system. It is one sitting, with statements you already have.
In a few minutes you will run this yourself. It is one subtraction, with numbers already printed on your own statements.

longo.sub: what came back, what went out
longo.nar: The calculation has two sides, and the common mistake is looking at only the first.
Side one is everything the card returned to you over twelve months. Cash back, statement credits, points you actually redeemed.
Points sitting unredeemed do not count. They are not money until you spend them, and plenty of them expire that way.
And when you do redeem points, value them at what you would otherwise have paid in cash. Not at the number the program shows you.
Side two is what holding the card cost you: the annual fee, and any fee you paid because of this card and not another.
Use the same twelve months on both sides. Mixing a full year of rewards with one month of fees proves whatever you already believed.
If a sign-up bonus landed in that window, keep it separate for now. It is real money, but it happens once and it distorts the picture.
Referral credits get the same treatment. Anything that will not repeat next year goes in its own line.
With both sides in the same unit and the same window, this stops being an opinion about cards and becomes arithmetic about your year.
So here is the math. One subtraction, and one optional division.
Step one: add up everything the card returned to you across those twelve months. Write it down.
Step two: add the annual fee and any fee that exists only because you hold this card. Write that down too.
Step three: subtract the second from the first. What is left is what the card actually paid you last year.
If the result is positive, that is real money the card handed you, and now you know the size of it instead of guessing.
If it is negative, that is what the card cost you to carry. Not a rate, not a percentage. A number, in your currency.
If you want it in monthly terms, divide by twelve. That makes it easier to compare with the other things you pay every month.
Four lines on paper is enough: rewards, fees, the difference, and the date the fee posts. That last line is what makes it actionable.
The math ends here and you can run yours now. The rest of this video is where the numbers hide, what the subtraction misses, and when it lies.
Now the part that makes people get this wrong: where those numbers are actually kept.
Most card issuers produce a year-end summary. Start there, because it collects twelve months in one place.
Then check it against your statements, because those summaries sometimes count only one category and quietly leave others out.
Watch for statement credits. They arrive looking like a discount on a purchase, so they are easy to miss on the rewards side.
The fee may not be labelled the way you expect, and on some cards it arrives split or waived for the first year only.
Charges that exist because of this card and not another belong on the cost side too. If another card in your wallet would not have charged it, it counts.
If the summary looks thin, open the twelve statements themselves. It takes twenty minutes and it removes all the guessing.
While you are in there, note the date the annual fee posted. That is your deadline for next year, and it is the one thing people never write down.
When you are unsure, undercount the rewards side. If the answer still looks good under a stingy count, it really is good.

longo.sub: and it is fair to say
longo.nar: There are things this subtraction does not capture, and it is more honest to name them than to pretend it settles everything.
The first: purchase and travel protections. They are worth something, and most people never use them.
Value them the way you would value insurance: by what you would have paid for the same cover, not by how long the feature list is.
The second cuts the other way. If chasing rewards made you spend more than you otherwise would, that difference belongs on the cost side.
That number is uncomfortable and rarely written down, but it is the one that turns a good-looking result into a bad year.
The third is simple. If you ever carried a balance on this card, interest goes on the cost side, and it usually dwarfs everything else here.
There is a fourth, smaller one: the time spent tracking categories and chasing redemptions. If that is hours a month, it belongs somewhere.
All of these belong AFTER the subtraction, never before it. Raised first, they become reasons not to look at the number at all.
In that case the rewards question is not the important one. The balance is, and no reward rate outruns it.
Now the case that fools almost everyone.
A first year is not a normal year. Sign-up bonuses and waived fees make the result look better than the card will ever look again.
If you have held the card longer than a year, run the calculation on a year with no bonus in it. That is the honest one.
An unusual year cuts the other way too. A year with one large purchase, or one you spent mostly at home, is not the year ahead either.
Two ordinary years are enough to tell whether you are looking at a pattern or at one strange twelve months.
And the choice is rarely just keep or cancel. Most issuers have a version of the same card with no fee, and moving to it is a third option.
That option also tends to preserve how long the account has been open, which some people care about for reasons outside this calculation.
There is usually a window after the fee posts in which the decision can still be reversed. Worth knowing before you need it.
Keeping the card and dropping it are both defensible, and neither is right in general. The right one is whatever your number points to. The only wrong move is renewing by default and never looking.
Now the step that makes the size of this feel real.
The difference in a single year usually looks small, in either direction. It is small, and that is exactly why it survives unexamined.

longo.preco: by the years you have held it
longo.nar: Multiply it by the number of years you have held the card. Same behaviour, added up.
Then look forward, because the fee repeats on a schedule and so does the result, with the same sign.

To feel the size, compare it with something familiar. If several years add up to a flight you would have taken anyway, that says one thing. If they add up to a coffee, that says something very different.
It is entirely possible the number comes out near zero, and nothing needs to change. That is a complete answer, and now it is measured rather than assumed.
Run this per card, not across your whole wallet. Two cards can pull in opposite directions, and averaging them hides both.
Two cards run side by side is usually enough to see which one is carrying the other.
The good part is that this decision returns every year, and returns whole. One bad year does not commit the next one.
We will close with what you can do today, in three steps.
First: add everything the card returned to you over twelve months. Second: add the annual fee and any fee that exists only because of this card. Third: subtract the second from the first.
Do it once, on last year, using the year-end summary as your starting point. It is one sitting.
If it comes out positive, you are done, and you can stop wondering about it every time the fee posts.
If it comes out negative, the decision now has a visible price. You are still allowed to pay it — the difference is that you know.
And if you do change something, change one thing: the card, or how you redeem. Changing both at once means you will never know which one worked.
And put the fee date somewhere you will actually see it, a month ahead. That single line is what turns this from a one-off into a decision.
If you run it, post one thing below: the result, with its sign. No card name, no balance, just the number. I want to see how far these spread between people holding the same kind of card.

short.nar: Your rewards card pays you back and charges you to hold it. Which one won last year? Run it now.
Number one: everything the card returned over twelve months. Cash back, statement credits, points you actually redeemed.
Number two: the annual fee, plus any fee that exists only because you hold this card.
Subtract the second from the first. Positive means the card paid you. Negative is what it cost you to carry. That is the whole calculation.

## AVISO SOBRE OS NUMEROS
Este video NAO cita nenhum numero meu e NAO faz nenhuma afirmacao institucional. Nao cita percentual de recompensa, nao cita valor de anuidade, nao cita taxa de juro, nao cita nome de banco, de cartao nem de programa de pontos, e nao compara produtos entre si.
